title: Helen Mirren is playing Patricia Highsmith?! Watch the trailer for  A Talent for Murder.
desc: This morning, fans of both Patricia Highsmith and Dame Helen Mirren have cause to rejoice. The trailer for Anton Corbijn’s new Ripley-adjacent film,A Taste for Murder, is out now.The film stars Alden ...
content:
This morning, fans of both Patricia Highsmith and Dame Helen Mirren have cause to rejoice. The trailer for Anton Corbijn’s new Ripley-adjacent film,A Taste for Murder, is out now.

The film stars Alden Ehrenreich, Olivia Cooke, and an almost unrecognizable Helen Mirren. It follows a thirsty agent (Ehrenreich) who heads to the Swiss hinterlands to convince Highsmith (Mirren!) to write one last installment of her famous Ripley series. But things—as they tend to, in the Highsmith universe—take a dark turn.

Here’s the trailer.

A Talent for Murderis itselfan adaptation,of the 2014 playSwitzerlandby Joanna Murray-Smith.Switzerlandimagines Highsmith as a recluse in the Alps, closely guarding a cache of weapons and secrets after a lifetime spent writing mysteries.

The play enjoyed runs in Bristol, Sydney, and Los Angeles. Murray-Smith is adapting her own script for the screen version.

This project joins a long line of Ripley adaptations. A bevy of international auteurs—including René Clément, Wim Wenders, and Anthony Minghella—have taken a pass at old Tom and his creator. The dark-hearted con man last received the screen treatment in a Netflix adaptation starring Andrew Scott. But we’reoriginalists, over here.

One thing’s certain. It will be exciting to see how a focus on Highsmith can draw some fresh blood from this story, which historically hinges on the magnetic cipher at its center. And obviously, we’ve gotta see whatDame Helen’sup to.

Look for the film in theaters on October 23.

title: An Ode to the Gleeful Terror of Tim Curry’s Pennywise
desc: Tim Curry, who died this week at 80, will probably always be best known for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter inThe Rocky Horror PictureShow, and not unreasonably. With his snug corset and unsubtl...
content:
Tim Curry, who died this week at 80, will probably always be best known for his performance as Dr. Frank-N-Furter inThe Rocky Horror PictureShow, and not unreasonably. With his snug corset and unsubtle make-up and minuscule shorts to which are fastened fishnet stockings, Curry’s kooky scientist with a penchant for  brewing male lovers in his lab is one of pop-culture’s unlikely icons. Frank-N-Furter exists in the gap between the counter culture and punk, the child of classic musicals and 1930s B-movies. The performance is daringly weird, perverse and outlandish, seductively charming, and, for all the flamboyance, Curry never veers out of control, never takes it too far. With his gender-defying garb and the way he gleefully flaunts his sexuality, Frank-N-Furter is an inimitable figure, unburdened by shame. And this strange, beseeching man who proudly eschews the mainstream’s prissy morals isn’t an outcast: he rules over a large, diverse assembly of hired help and acolytes who seem, largely, tolikehim. In any case, they’re content enough spontaneously break into carefully choreographed musical numbers. He’s a mad scientist, but Curry plays him as something more interesting, somethingweirder, than a villain.

Curry’s genius is that he shows us how fun and liberating embracing the weird can be. He admires how the Transylvanian just acts like himself. But my favorite Tim Curry performance will always be Pennywise, the clown in Tommy Lee Wallace’s 1990 miniseries adaptation of Stephen King’sIt, which, compared to Andy Muschietti’s mega popular pair of films, is modest, even a little lame. The miniseries is only three hours long, so Wallace had to heavily truncate King’s gargantuan tome, curtailing and expunging scenes and entire characters, as well as toning things down to fit broadcast rules.

But Wallace uses this hindrance as inspiration for creative ways of translating King’s writing to the small screen. You can see it from the very beginning. The first chapter of the novel is one of the scariest things King has ever written. It’s smartly structured, the details with which he describes the scene are astute and intense, the prose is lovely and melancholy and mostly free of the sloppy redundancies and annoying colloquial tics that King loves a little too much, the two young brothers are efficiently and empathetically fleshed out so we are quickly invested in them, and when the horror, which he portends, does arrive, it’s not just shocking, but tragic. The miniseries is basically the same.

It’s a rainy day, and a young boy wearing a yellow raincoat chases a boat made of newspaper floating down a gutter alive with flowing rain. The boat falls into a sewer, and, as the boy goes to retrieve it, a face appears out of darkness—a clown, with spotless, uncanny white skin, a bulbous red nose, and untamed red hair. In his Bronx accent, he talks affably to the boy, magnanimously returning his boat and asking him to play. Soon enough, he tears the boy’s arm off and leaves him to die in the gutter. In the miniseries, this is implied, following the decree of network TV standards circa 1990, but it’s still scary because Curry almost convinces us that he is a nice clown, a friend, even though he is lurking in a sewer. When his insidious nature is revealed, the change in tone and his face gone malformed, the scene feels dynamic in a way that doesn’t require gore or intricate special effects. Here and throughout the film, we see how he has fun betraying a child’s trust and ruining his innocence, which is maybe an even more profound violence than dismemberment. The shape-shifting eldritch entity of mysterious origins relishes torturing children. He takes many forms, but likes being a clown the best. It’s a nasty irony. As King writes, “The fears of children could often be summoned up in a single face… and if bait were needed, why, what child did not love a clown?”

“The clown may be the source of mirth, but—who shall make the clown laugh?” Angela Carter wrote inNights at the Circus. Pennywise, naturally, makes himself laugh.

While Muschietti’s films are far more faithful translations of King’s opus narratively, having the freedom of an R rating, a big budget, and twice as much time as the miniseries to tell the story, they rely on generic creepy imagery and ostentatious scare tactics, expensive banality. Bill Skarsgård plays Pennywise with relentless menace. There is little nuance and few surprises. Compare Curry’s Pennywise to Bill Skarsgård’s: Skarsgård looks and sounds unequivocally evil from the beginning, whereas Curry actually has the mannerisms of a clown you might find at a kid’s backyard birthday party. That juxtaposition makes him scary and exciting. Curry knew that in order to scare kids, he first has to appeal to them, inveigle them with his deceitful promise of friendship, earn their trust with kindness, all smiles, and speak to them in playful words—speak their own language. As Lovecraft says in “The Outsider,” “Unhappy is he to whom the memories of childhood bring only fear and sadness.” This may be why as adults, the Losers Club forget their childhood horrors: so they can save their own lives. If you can’t get your innocence back, maybe you can at least rid yourself of the memory of what took it from you.

And, unlike Bill Skarsgård’s, Curry’s Pennywise is having fun. His taunts and emotional torture are unsettling yet also profane fun because he delivers them in the tone of a friend busting your chops. When he appears in the library, invisible to all but our lead character, he has a hoot practicing his standup. “The clown may be the source of mirth, but—who shall make the clown laugh?” Angela Carter wrote inNights at the Circus. Pennywise, naturally, makes himself laugh.

The image of him, his attire a blasphemous betrayal of the wholesome fun a clown costume promises, and with vibrant, colorful balloons in his hand, lingers in our minds for a long time. He appears on screen for less than 20 minutes, yet it feels like he is always there. In his absence, we still sense his danger. He is all the characters think about.

We can contrast Curry’s clown to another supernatural villain he played, Darkness inLegend, mythic under the prosthetics, delivering in his deep demonic voice cryptic proclamations. And yet, Darkness has a romantic side, too: he is attracted to the innocence of a beautiful young woman, and wants to marry her. (Though he uses dark magic to woo her, which to him is an acceptable declaration of love.) When he is vanquished at the end, he reminds Tom Cruise’s hero that evil lurks in all living things, so while his corporeal presence may die, his essence lives on.

Pennywise—or rather, It—has terrorized the small simple town of Derry, Maine for who knows how long, generation after generation born and dead as he remains lurking in nightmares, manipulating his victims, making real their deepest fears because he knows them so well. King’s best writing has an earnest intimacy. What makes him one of the great writers of adolescents is the respect with which he portrays the kids’ vulnerable moments, their hopes, their shame, their fears.

Too often, horror has gradually come to think that if a film wants to be taken seriously, its bad guys, however wicked, however sadistic, man or monster, whatever their motivation (if they even have one), should be austere. Humor is unbecoming. Tim Curry had no such delusions; he understood that scary can be fun, and fun can provoke fear. When Pennywise cracks a joke, the contrast of his antics with the scary stuff can be more impactful, have more personality, than just scare after scare. It’s a skill to control tone and tempo and cadence. And when Pennywise enjoys the horror he evokes, his laugh can perturb more deeply and last more clearly in your memory than a simple jumpscare or spilled blood. You don’t forget Pennywise telling a kid, “Kiss me, fat boy!” and neither does the kid, who is embarrassed by his weight, gets teased about it; years later, as a slender, successful adult, when the long-buried memories of Derry come back, it’s that quip and the clown’s guffaw he remembers.

title: If You Build It, Will They Come? On the Sperm Racing World Cup
desc: Ghadeer Bustani,CC BY-SA 4.0, viaWikimedia Commons.In 1677, a medical student named Johann Ham approached the Dutch scientist and future “Father of Microbiology” Antonie van Leeuwenhoek with unsettlin...
content:
Ghadeer Bustani,CC BY-SA 4.0, viaWikimedia Commons.

In 1677, a medical student named Johann Ham approached the Dutch scientist and future “Father of Microbiology” Antonie van Leeuwenhoek with unsettling news: there were tiny creatures living in his semen. Or not inhissemen, not necessarily. Some incorrigible friend—someone who certainly wasn’t Ham—had dislodged his wad in the company of an “unclean woman” and then transferred custody of his deposit by means unattested into Ham’s hands. Curious Ham had splashed the discharge under a microscope and, startled by its contents, brought his discovery and its medium to Van Leeuwenhoek for a second opinion. Examining the sample, the renowned microscopist, who had already described what we call red blood cells and protists in pioneering detail, glimpsed spindly tailed animalcules moving in the muck. He proceeded to set about procuring new goo from a close, morally uncompromised source. “What I here describe was not obtained by any sinful contrivance on my part, but the observations were made upon the excess with which Nature provided me in my conjugal relations,” he wrote some months later to the Royal Society of London regarding the remains of an emission he’d slathered under his powerful single-lens microscope.

I relate this lightly editorialized and moderately abridged history of the identification of what would become known as spermatozoa because it marks the first time that a man had cause and the capability to wonder at the meaning of the living contents of his ejaculate—and thus to search his little reflecting pool for the secrets of humanity, of himself. And because, in 2024, some 347 years after Van Leeuwenhoek fired his fateful blast, a money-minded form of this fascination prompted a team of teenage and early-twenties shitpost entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley to found a sports start-up calledSperm Racing. It has raised $10 million in funding.

The company first came to my attention this February, a month before it was due to roll out an ambitious Sperm Racing World Cup featuring contestants representing 128 countries. When an editor for this magazine asked me to write about the championship, I began to picture myself as an anxious, anthropomorphized gamete paddling desperately toward its subject, its theme, its egg, endeavoring to fulfill its purpose, to conceive a story. Come is, as it happens, a subject on which I enjoy some expertise. Through the power of the internet and promiscuity, I’ve learned to appreciate the rich diversity of whitish matter the human body can produce. Color, velocity, viscosity, volume, reach, and duration differ from person to person, from shot to shot. I’ve become familiar with the venerable tradition, staged between men (and not only men) every day, of exhibition, comparison, and analysis, in which the relation between the two parties, or between one’s fantasy and one’s reality, or between one’s present output and one’s memory of past productions, adds to the pleasure that inheres in the act itself.

Sperm Racing is, more or less, a scientized and de-eroticized update on this “venerable tradition.” At the Sperm Racing headquarters in San Francisco, two contestants donate their semen, which is centrifugally cleaned; healthy sperm are isolated from the samples; and the cells then race through courses less than a half-centimeter long that are etched into microfluidic silicon chips. The sperm are pipetted into warm liquid currents designed to mimic the reproductive environment; these currents allow the cells to orient themselves in the faux canal, such that the cells begin to swim upstream, as they would against the flow of mucus in a vagina, toward the finish line. (Until recently, the company’s chief science officer was a teenager named Rishi Kanaparti, whose past work includes papers on, among other things, “Motion Resilient Deep Learning for ECG Signal Classification.”) The raw footage is boring and difficult for the human eye to parse—vaguely defined blobs move against a white background—so the company’s computers track the cells’ coordinates and generate visual approximations of the contests. They then debut these videos at occasional live events, like one that pitted a USC student against a UCLA student last April, and post them on social media. Several Reels on Instagram feature a bellowing commentator who goes by BSTCHLD. “This is a microscopic masterclass,” BSTCHLD shouts during one blowout. As a sperm enters the end zone: “INSEMINATION!”

In preparing for the World Cup, I imagined how I might engage my subject. I could follow the matches as they unfolded. I would attend a race if possible; I might host a watch party; I might gather some gays at my house to shoot rope on camera for an unaffiliated competition during the watch party. Sperm Racing could beget fagslop. I had thoughts. I had plans. They would, at length, go somewhat bust.

One such plan: In the spirit of participatory journalism, I applied to the Sperm Racing World Cup a few days after receiving this assignment, assuming that I would be screened out for being old (thirty-three), common (American), and of no particular repute as a content creator and thus of no particular value to a would-be sport whose founders require significant reserves of the public’s attention for their goop regatta saga to succeed. I answered questions about my ancestry, diet, workout frequency and routine, and motivations (options included “fertility awareness” and “national pride”). I dutifully took screenshots of the Sperm Racing webpage and forwarded them to my editor. I scoured my inbox for a form email explaining my unworthiness—“Do Not Come,” its subject line might have read—but found nothing. I waited.

Onto Sperm Racing’s elegantly vulgar premise, the company has grafted a lame higher purpose intended to justify and temper the joyful adolescent stupidity of the enterprise. Sperm Racing’s website features a manifesto written in the tricolon-rich, not-this-but-that style of LLMs: “sperm racingisn’t just a joke. it’s not just some viral idea for the internet to laugh at.it’s something much bigger.” (The bolding and highlighting are in the original manifesto.) It’s about men’s health and male fertility, apparently. A widely cited review of medical literature published in 2022 found that sperm concentration had declined by more than 50 percent globally over the preceding fifty years, and reasonable concerns about the effects of ultra-processed foods, pesticides, and other environmental and social ills on gametes pervade theMAHAsphere and beyond. (At least one more recent study found no significant changes in potency among otherwise fertile American men, and a much-discussedFinancial Timesarticlefrom May presented an analysis of data that compellingly advances the thesis that social isolation resulting from smartphone use may be the single greatest cause of declining birthrates.)

Sperm Racing is also about moving product: The company has sold plastic-free boxer-briefs under the brand nameAndros, as well as supplements calledSperm Worms, whose website promises “better tasting loads, fertility support, and daily performance in four gummies a day.” Or, per Sam Kriss, who described the company and its now-eighteen-year-old founder Eric Zhu in a FebruaryHarper’sdispatch on Silicon Valley, it’s about attention arbitrage. “Sperm Racing seemed to be first and foremost a social media hype machine,” Kriss wrote. “A third of Eric’s staff work on videos, producing a seemingly endless stream of viral content.”

Put another way, Sperm Racing is about future anxiety, the fetish for self-optimization, and the drive to monetize people’s fears and weaknesses, not least their screen habits. (Sperm Racing’s videos are part of a larger crop of social media spermslop that includes, for example, an AI-generatedvideoof a mournful spermatozoa being tortured by a smoldering cigarette and heckled by a hotdog and a hamburger.) But to the company’s credit, people have been asking the questions its project poses for centuries—or anyway, they resonated with me. Questions like: Are the contents of my person inadequate? Am I incapable of producing anything worthwhile? Are my devices futile?

In March, during a break at work, I interviewed one of Sperm Racing’s cofounders, a twenty-three-year-old named Shane Fan, an attention economy and crypto entrepreneur who commands millions of followers across social media platforms and calls himself an “internet detective.” It was Zhu who had come up with the comesports idea back in 2024, Fan said. The pair now wanted Sperm Racing “to be one of the world’s biggest sports.” He also told me that sperm hardiness can affect “a child’s immune health as well as a woman’s pregnancy experience,” and that the World Cup had been delayed. (“We will start having the first events in early April,” he said.) I waited for him to mention my application or to laugh it off. Meek or distracted, I did not raise it myself, but learned that Andros’s underwear is “designed to reduce microplastics in your balls, as well as heat and friction.”

April arrived. The World Cup didn’t. In emails, Fan assured me that later in the month—and then later still—he would share a schedule. Soon I learned that the Cup had been pushed back further. An article about Sperm Racing that appeared inThe Daily Mailnear the end of the month mentioned a May start date and applications from “the US, Iran, Israel, and even North Korea.” But no action occurred; there was no fap nor any opportunity to stage an orgiastic screening; there was nothing but an implacable urge to describe myself as having been edged and teased. My follow-up emails had stopped receiving responses. Perhaps I was a slow sperm or a broken-tailed one, destined to spin upon myself. Perhaps I would have to make the brave and healthful decision of prioritizing my own sclerosis in the narrative: perhaps I would have to write a personal essay, or to think aloud about the relationship between writing and coming. What writer has not wished his emissions came in greater volume and frequency; that if witnesses to his works were not born anew or overawed—that if his salvos did not literally beget life in readers—they might still please his audience? It seemed the World Cup and I had both been forgotten. We had been lost in the sauce.

Then, one day in May, a possible explanation for Sperm Racing’s radio silence appeared in my inbox courtesy of a Google Alert: The company, it appeared, was rebranding as part of an effort to de-emphasize the childishness of its premise and attract millennial and zillennial viewers—a cohort that might be actively trying to sire children, and thus one that might be expected to fret about sperm health. As a symbol of their new maturity, they were considering jettisoning the name Sperm Racing entirely, in favor of the more staid trade-name, “Biomarker Sports.” I’d learned all this from a feature inThe New YorkTimes Magazine,whose author, Daniel Waite Penny, had, it seemed, been granted extensive access to Sperm Racing’s facilities and personnel and who had actually gotten to compete in—and win—a race. In the shadow of Penny’s piece, I worried I had been jerked around by nutjobs, that my piece was a bust, that no amount of belabored wordplay would rescue me from dread anticlimax. But the ultimate anticlimax was yet to come.

In June I received an email from Shane. He wanted to talk—he said he had a lead for me. On a call, he told me that in just three weeks’ time, on the eve of Independence Day, Sperm Racing would at last stage a contest that he described as “an inaugural match for the World Cup as well as Biomarker Sports.” Julius Ritter, a twenty-five-year-old venture capitalist and peptide enthusiast from Germany who also works in AI, would compete against twenty-seven-year-old Jayden Clark, an all-natural, iron-pumping jazz musician with “sub-10-percent body fat” (per Fan) from Australia. A question few had been asking—Are one fit biohacker’s sperm quicker than those of a guy who just spends a lot of time lifting and gorging on boy kibble?—would be answered. “We want our next event to be really, really serious,” Fan said.

That date came and went too. Finally, on July 12, the night after theFIFAWorld Cup quarterfinals, I sequestered myself in a dim bedroom at the back of a house in Fire Island Pines and stared bleary-eyed at my computer screen. At the stated start time of 8P.M.the stream remained dead. Updates were issued via Instagram Story—the race would now kick off at 9P.M.—and trickled into agitated comment sections on YouTube and Twitch. Four days into a bender, I felt like degraded biological material crusting on a blanket. My body, and likely my boys, was reeling; the orgiastic spectacle I had hoped might carry over into a watch party had concluded twelve hours prior, at a new friend’s compound, after he’d booted the men still chatting or swapping biomarkers around his pool; all joy had gone from the world. “Blue balls,” I thought dreamily as I waited for kickoff.

When the event did commence, at 9:30P.M.Eastern, an hour and a half after its appointed time, an introductory video made the case for Sperm Racing’s place in the lineage of Silicon Valley movers and shakers. Images of Steve Jobs, Elon Musk, and the San Francisco skyline filled my monitor. “Tonight,” a voiceover relayed, “this city becomes the birthplace of something entirely new: health entertainment.” Then the venue came into view: three blazered commentators—one of them Nick Small, another teenage Sperm Racing cofounder—sat behind a gray anchor desk decorated with Sperm Racing’s name and logo. (The Biomarker Sports rebrand seemed to have been forgotten.) Behind them, at the back of a minimalist studio space, lurked a large screen showing Ritter and Clark’s frozen visages in half-shadow; bio storage lockers lined one wall, while several metal lightbox tables flush with scientific equipment stood around the floor.

Over the course of the event, a mustachioed spokesman conducted brief video interviews with aged physicians, and Sperm Racing’s bio team milled around between pipette stations and microscopes, supposedly preparing brews freshly jettisoned by the Australian and the German for competition. The panel of three commentators leaned forward to read in stilted cadences from a laptop positioned between them and issued tepid pronouncements about T levels and other player stats, their audio meanwhile going in and out. Twice the cameras cut to darkened rooms, leaving the host—one Ricky Del Rosario, a keynote speaker, auctioneer, and certified life coach who alone exuded professionalism and ease in front of the cameras—and pundits to beseech their techs to flip the lights on. Amateurish and tiresome, the affair seemed to have been conducted for the sole purpose of clipfarming it for social media after the fact. “We are the lucky ones,” Del Rosario said, paraphrasingRichard Dawkins, near the end of a would-be soaring monologue about the unlikelihood of being alive that has since been edited into aviralvideo. “We are the ones who get to die, because we are the ones who got to be born.” Hype reels for the company and the two blonde, short-king contestants flashed across my MacBook’s screen: “Yeah, I think I might be the happiest person alive,” Clark, the Australian, said in one. An ad for Brex, a fintech company, played for the approximately 150 people who were watching the live stream on YouTube at any given time. (Others watched on Twitch and Kick.) Near the end of the sub-sixty-minute boondoggle, the tripart race ensued, with sperm concentration and something called a “full-field competition” supplementing the classic sprint. Do you care who won? I didn’t.1I was glad when it was over.

Nonetheless, sperm racing’s seed is spreading, and an imitator could have better luck. That appears to be the hope of Luke Hawash, a twentysomething AI game developer who uses the social media handle @mr.spermracing and goes by the nom de come “Dick Gay.” Formerly the chief marketing officer for Sperm Racing HQ, Gay-Hawash now refers to himself as the division president for a rival franchise called “Spermrace Asia.” Earlier this month, he hosted what was billed as Asia’s first sperm race in Hong Kong for a crowd that reportedly numbered in the hundreds. Fan seemed less than thrilled: “That is not affiliated with us,” he wrote in an email, “so I cannot comment on that.”

From a certain point of view, Sperm Racing is advancing a kind of radical introspection. Look inside yourself, the company says. Now externalize this hidden part of yourself, this physical instance of your interiority. Subject it to inspection, measurement, and public judgment. Learn if you are dead inside or bursting with life; learn how your exercise regimen, your diet and drug habits, your peptide stack, your age and income redound upon your gametes’ ability to fertilize an egg and thus upon your potency—with all that word’s interrelated and stirring meanings obtaining—and thus upon your status as a man. But from another point of view—from mine, watching the stream on my computer—the World Cup’s innovation, and the disruption Sperm Racing has created in the marketplace of semen production, is to make ejaculation and its contemplation boring. Eros never stood a chance, but I’d thought that Van Leeuwenhoek and Ham’s wonder and curiosity might find purchase on the broadcast. Alas, the proof is in the pudding, so to speak.

[1]It was the plucky Australian—a victory for gym-rat saxophonists everywhere.

Paul McAdory is a writer from Mississippi. He lives in Brooklyn.

title: The Catalogue of Lost Things
desc: Every month,our desks at theReviewpile up with dozens of soon-to-be published books, only some of which involve writers we have heard of, or subjects we know anything about. More often, we wind up wit...
content:
Every month,our desks at theReviewpile up with dozens of soon-to-be published books, only some of which involve writers we have heard of, or subjects we know anything about. More often, we wind up with a mix somewhere between that of a cabinet of curiosities and a Little Free Library stocked by an indecisive grad student; this summer, for example, alongside many debut novels and NYRB reissues, we found an Italian chapbook of cat-themed poems from the eighties and a semiepistolary critique of psychiatry whose letters are addressed “Dear Neoliberalism.” While combing through these galleys for good ideas or good writing, I sometimes save passages I like. Here are a few I found in July and August.

—Tarpley Hitt, online editor

In our Spring 2024 issue, we published a story by Joanna Kavenna called “The Beautiful Salmon,” about a philosophy student who goes to a dinner party at the house of a “brilliant and terrifying” professor, who has cooked a beautiful salmon. A version of that story appears inSeven: or, How to Play a Game Without Rules(Faber & Faber), Kavenna’s sly and dextrous new novel about the same student and the same professor, who specializes in something called “Box Philosophy,” short for “Thinking outside the Box about Thinking outside the Box.”

At one point, the professor sends the student to Greece to track down a “poet-dentist” named Apostolakis, who is “tangentially linked to Box Philosophy,” but has lately been working on a book he’s calling theFanouropiton,or theCatalogue of Lost Things:

The book was divided into short entries, like an encyclopaedia.Things Lost by War. Things Lost by Human Folly. Things Lost Because No One Really Cared About Them.And,Things Lost Because Too Many People Cared About Them—a category full of betrayals and thefts. One entry inThings You’d Assume Were Too Big to Get Lostdescribed an entire galaxy that shone approximately 2.5 million times brighter than the sun, but when various distinguished astronomers gathered to examine it further, they found it had disappeared. No one knew why—they would have needed to find it again to answer the question of why it had vanished.

In an email I received about a new book by the author A. Igoni Barrett, his agent succinctly summed upBlackass, Barrett’s debut novel from 2016, as follows:“Ayoung man named Furo Wariboko woke up one morning in Lagos to find that he had transformed into a white man. Except for his ass.”

This is the epigraph to Barrett’s follow-up,Whyteface(Greywolf):

Please don’t peace here—WORDS SCRAWLED IN PAINT ON A PISS-STAINED WALL SOMEWHERE IN NIGERIA

Claire Carusillo—who recently chronicled her first month running a combination bookstore-skate-shop in Utah in adiaryfor theDaily—wrote a novel calledThe Responsible Party(Henry Holt), in which a protagonist, also named Claire Carusillo, untangles a complex family history involving several sinking ships, a mother-daughter duo who made it big in the regional vaudeville circuit, and a murder. Here’s a paragraph about one branch of the family tree:

As a girl, my great-grandmother Dag exuded that same toxic chromium-6 glow as the perfect tens I grew up with a hundred years later. Like those dime pieces, Dag was astonishingly beautiful for Illinois and still pretty good by coastal standards, and so secure in her wherewithal to fellate any male school instructor under fifty that she never worried about participation points. And if you think I sound bitter because I wasn’t popular enough to get teen pregnant or so drunk that I crashed a Jet Ski into a floating hot dog stand during after-prom weekend, then you misunderstand me. Bully for them. I was busy back then, exfoliating my chin and decorating my laptop with puffy stickers.

Rosalind Belben’sIs Beauty Goodwas originally published in 1989, and is probably a novel, though one would be forgiven for mistaking it for a collection of stories, poems, very long koans, or, as Esther Kinsky puts it in her introduction to a new reissue (NYRB Classics), “fairy-tale pebbles.” From a chapter called “The Shy Elt”:

She has sold all our assets & squandrd the proceedsa child cld tell her that is !!false econ. I AM perturbd.

The endnotes of Lee Cadesky’sGrub: Why We Eat, Why It Matters, and the Seven Forces That Shape Our Food(Prometheus) include an appendix titled “A Brief and Selected Chemistry of Water”:

The atoms in water arrange themselves in a very specific way. Oxygen sits at the center of the molecule, reaching out in either direction to hold on to a hydrogen atom. Oxygen has two pairs of electrons that sit on its back side and two remaining electrons that each share themselves with a hydrogen atom to create a covalent chemical bond. This gives the water molecule a little kink.

We Were Forbidden(Transit) includes three short stories by Jacqueline Harpman, the late Belgian author ofI Who Have Never Known Men, in translation byRos Schwartz.From the opening of the second story, “The Outcast”:

Henriette Serrano and I were fifteen and we were friends. We would talk nonstop, mostly about literature, but we weren’t afraid to tackle any of the big issues facing humanity. We discussed the existence of God, the meaning of life, human destiny and who was likely to win the war … In 1942, after the American landing in Casablanca, Henriette switched allegiance from Pétain to De Gaulle. I tactfully refrained from comment.

Emily Eakin’sThe Frenchmen: Or, My Life In Theory(Penguin Press) is something like a group biography, though one whose eight subjects—the French theorists Louis Althusser, Roland Barthes, Gilles Deleuze, Michel Foucault, Félix Guattari, Jacques Derrida, and Jacques Lacan, as well as one Belgian (Paul de Man)—largely agreed the author was dead. Derrida, for example, once told an interviewer that “sometimes the one who reads a text by a philosopher, for instance a tiny paragraph, and interprets it in a rigorous, inventive, and powerfully deciphering fashion is more of a real biographer than the one who knows the whole story.”

Nevertheless, Eakin’s biographical research yields many tiny paragraphs worth unpacking:

In some ways the École Normale hadn’t changed much since Althusser first saw it. The menu at thepot—the cafeteria—had no doubt improved; when Derrida was a student, he filed a formal complaint about the food, objecting to the mushy peas and the Camembert that approached “the consistency of brick.”

Ivan Turgenev’sSmoke,newly translated by Donald Rayfield (NYRB Classics), was panned by his peers for its scathing depiction of Russian expats, prompting him to add a foreword—which, in this copy, appears at the end:

In view of the very various negative comments to which the taleSmokehas been subjected, some of the author’s friends have advised him to equip its edition in book form with a foreword, in which he would try to clear up any misunderstandings that have arisen. But after mature consideration of the matter, the author did not think it necessary to follow this advice.

title: James Joyce’s Baby Impressions and Other “Awkward Pleasures” of Literary Biography
desc: In the Lake District, 1994.Each week,The Paris Reviewunlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive.This week, we’ve unlocked ourinterviewwith Hermione Lee, selected from the ...
content:
In the Lake District, 1994.

Each week,The Paris Reviewunlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive.This week, we’ve unlocked ourinterviewwith Hermione Lee, selected from the archive by Daisy Hildyard, whose story “Two Lives” appears in our recent Summer issue. Sign up for theReduxnewsletter to receive these pieces to your inbox every Sunday morning.

Everybody dabbles in biography. If you have ever spoken at a funeral, rewritten your CV, or gossiped, you’ve had to deal with some of the questions that Hermione Lee discusses with Louisa Thomas in herArt of Biographyinterview. What is the shape of a life? What are the ingredients of an achievement? What specific person and what particular circumstances produced it? When something fails, do we have to find somebody to blame? Lee addresses these questions as matters of technique: the work of finding, or inventing, “a structure that is sympathetic to the subject.”

There is a kind of mise en abyme at play in her work, and in this interview about the life of somebody who writes the lives of those who captured something of life in their writing. Literary biography is an awkward pleasure. I like its strange textures and surprises. You catch James Joyce doing his impressions of a baby, or spend the summer with Tolstoy when he is on one of his horse yogurt diets. I believed I had a fair understanding of W. G. Sebald until I read his biography and saw the black-and-white snapshot of him as a young man standing thigh-deep in a river, topless in wet jeans with a deep tan, defined muscles, and a dagger in his hand. I also enjoy the genre for its practical insights. It’s useful to know how other writers chased their invoices, or when their children napped.

Lee’s biographies are exceptional for their integration of original research with illuminating interpretations of the authors’ works, and they last. I’ve read and reread herPenelope FitzgeraldandVirginia Woolf; I’ve used the footnotes and followed her sources. I still have my mother’s twenty-nine-year-old Virago Press paperbackWilla Cather. I can’t think of another writer, biographer or otherwise, who reads as closely as Lee, or with the same balance and imagination.

In their searching conversation, I was particularly interested in what Lee and Thomas have to say about the undisclosed elements of a life, including Lee’s own (she is reticent). They discuss lies and secrets. They also discuss inventiveness and hard work. The interview leaves me with a sense of how much it takes to make a sincere attempt to understand another person’s life.

The Art of Biography No. 4Hermione Lee, interviewed by Louisa Thomas

Do you find that you read biographies and think, This person is falling in love with his or her subject?

There are some figures, aren’t there, who seem to attract a certain kind of emotive treatment. Woolf is certainly one of them, Plath is another, Lawrence is another. Or, biography can be a form of rescue operation, special pleading.Painted Shadow: A Life of Vivienne Eliot, by Carole Seymour-Jones, is a good example of that. It has to demonize T. S. Eliot in order to do its job of rescuing his first wife. Biography has so much to do with blame. It is not a neutral zone. So you will get biographies of Woolf where Leonard is blamed, or where her half brothers, George and Gerald Duckworth, are blamed, or where her father, Leslie Stephen, is blamed. It’s as if you can’t tell a life story without someone having to be blamed. Named and shamed and blamed.

From issue no. 205 (Summer 2013)

title: In the Studio with Chad Fore, the Writer Behind “Lil Spooky”
desc: Photograph by Kathleen McNamara.In the time between his first submission to theReview,inFebruary oflast year, and the publication of his short story “Lil Spooky” in our newSummer issue, the writer Cha...
content:

In the time between his first submission to theReview,inFebruary oflast year, and the publication of his short story “Lil Spooky” in our newSummer issue, the writer Chad Fore and I exchanged almost a hundred emails. I also read several of his stories, which tend to be somewhat autobiographical, at least in the sense that they often take place in one of Fore’s two neighboring hometowns—Piru and Fillmore, in Southern California—and are rich with the kinds of details and characters that feel impossible to invent. “Lil Spooky” follows its high-school-age protagonist, Brad Camacho, through his gradual—then all too fast—initiation into a local gang. In a humiliation ritual disguised as a tryout, he has to freestyle for members of the gang’s hip-hop arm, also known as the Sick Minded Clique, which records posse cuts in a “decrepit old shack” they call the studio, at the end of one of their driveways. Knowing what I did about Fore’s fiction, I wasn’t entirely surprised when, alongside the first draft of this story, he included thelinkto a song he was featured on when he himself was in high school. He and I talked about the musical influences of his characters and of his own past over lunch this spring, when, after all those messages, we were finally able to meet in person. I found he has an encyclopedic memory for rap verses, some by artists we both love, and others that he’s been writing in his head, he said, for twenty years.

While we were editing “Lil Spooky,” you told me it was partly inspired by time you spent with your older cousin’s rap group in the nineties and early aughts. What drew you to that specific experience as a subject and how did you approach writing about it after so many years?

From the start I had in mind the type of story I wanted to write. When I think of friends from my hometown or family members who got involved in gangs or drugs or whatever—there were always opportunities before it got bad, where they could still get out of it. But then something happens, and they can’t anymore. I wanted the story to end at that moment where, without having been told anything, the reader would know that Brad’s in a different place, and now it is too late. There was one sentence that I almost cut. I went back and forth. Does this explain too much? Does it not explain enough?

“It was all pretend until the moment it wasn’t.” At a certain point you’ve fallen through the hole. That was the feeling I was trying to reproduce.

One thing that’s been on my mind is why it was attractive—the gang. The attitude toward things like gangs that I hear where I live now in Arizona is like, Why the hell would people ever do that? If people are stupid enough to join a gang, then who cares? Arrest them all. Let them kill each other.

In a way, it is hard to understand why someone would join a gang. But having grown up in that environment, I’m just like, Gangsters were the coolest people. They were the most popular. They got all the girls. Everyone looked up to them slash lived in fear of them. If you’re in a setting where everyone’s saying, This is cool, then it is cool. Anybody would think it’s cool. You’re in this world. This is what you might do.

In the story, there’s a sense of aspiration that I think ties in well with the music. I’m curious how the music plays into the story for you. You said your cousin had a rap group back in the day. That song that you sent—

Yeah. I’ve listened to it a number of times. So was there a “hip-hop arm” of the gang in real life?

I conflated the gang and the rap group a little bit. Some people who were involved in the rap group were also involved in the life. But I was not a gangster growing up. I did well in school, which made me not popular. I was on the basketball team. There was this one dude who was a fantastic rapper. He’s the first guy on “Flow Trip.” His name was Mikey. He’s got that gruff voice. I remember him in the studio being like, “We have to live it. We have to live the life if we’re rapping about it.” I felt that as a response to me in a way. I was kind of like Brad. Hip-hop in general, you’re rapping at a hypothetical enemy. You’re boasting. “I’d kick your ass.” I had never really done those things in my life.

The story exaggerates the attachment of the group to the gang, but at the same time there were gangs that had—you can find this online—rappers associated with them. Even in just this town of ten thousand people, there were probably a dozen active rap groups. A lot of it is gangbanging on wax. They’re making threats. My cousin’s rap group, not quite so much.

Are you the hook on “Flow Trip”?

That’s me singing it, yeah. My cousin knew I could sing, which was also not cool.

Listen, it’s not bad.

Not bad, but it’s also pretty crushing when you show up and it’s like, “You’re singing.” You know what I mean? I wanted to be a rapper. They gave me a lot of shit about it too. I remember Mikey was like, “Your name is gonna be Silky Chad. You’re not going to be C-4, you’re going to be Silky Chad.”

In what you would call gangster rap—that’s never a term I’ve used because it feels like something they would say on the news. “Oh, these gangster rappers …”

C. Delores Tucker, that congresswoman who was always bashing rap in the nineties, would use that term.

Yeah. But there is a real artistry to the way violence is depicted by the best rappers of that genre. I was just thinking about this line inLiquid Swords, the perfect album.

Don’t even—it’s so crazy you say that, because the GZA might be my favorite rapper of all time.

He’s unbelievable. But there’s that line—I think it’s in “Gold”—about waiting for the subway to pass and make enough noise so he can shoot this person without anyone hearing. There’s something about the way that he conveys it that makes you believe it’s something he’s actually done.

You said a lot right there. I’ve been thinking about why hip-hop was so important to me. Why was I so obsessed with it growing up? The lyrics are amazing. I teach rhetoric. I’m always talking about how writing is ethos, pathos, and logos. The rhetorical triangle. I was readingAPortrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and they have this discussion about the question of what beauty is in art. Stephen Dedalus is talking about Thomas Aquinas. Aquinas’s definition of beauty in art is that it has to have wholeness, harmony, and radiance. And then Dedalus describes radiance as a light that shines from another world. What he’s trying to say is it has to be good on a technical level, but it also has to have something else—some true sense of what the artist’s life is like.

Then, what did hip-hop stop doing for me? Why literary fiction? When I taught beginning creative writing, my students were like, “Why is every story sad?” Whereas, in certain kinds of hip-hop, there’s just the side that’s beating your chest. “I’m the best. I will kill you.” It’s missing some of life, where you’re alone with loss or vulnerability. That kind of hip-hop really resonated with thirteen-year-old me, who wanted to feel confident. I didn’t want to feel scared, so I wanted music that wasn’t scared. But my older self was like, Iamscared. I want to hear someone say that.

Fear is a rare emotion to hear in music.

Absolutely. That’s why I like “Tha Crossroads,” Bone Thugs-N-Harmony. That song came out after my grandma died. My sister wouldn’t listen to it. It was too sad.

Wasn’t that song about Eazy-E dying ofAIDS? Horrifyingly scary, especially at that time.

Speaking of the transition from trying to be badass to making art about however you are feeling—Bone Thugs-N-Harmony were protégés of Eazy-E, some of the hardest-core rappers of all time. There was literal Devil worship in their songs—“Mr. Ouija” onCreepin on Ah Come Up.Imagine my parents when they caught me with that. “What are they rapping about?” “Well, Devil worship.” I wasn’t allowed to buy CDs with the “explicit lyrics” stickers on them. So I would find CDs with stickers that you could take off. That’s how I wound up with a really weird collection. It was whatever I could peel off.

When you think about the time in which this story takes place, in Southern California in the late nineties, it’s immediately post-Biggie and Tupac.Life After Deathhas come out. Who was big for you?

It’s a good question. It was Cypress Hill. Because this is a Mexican community, ninety-nine percent Mexican. Latino rap was huge. Kid Frost, Delinquent Habits. The Mexakinz was a group. Even more regional, Lil Rob, and this guy Cowboy, who was a producer. One of the members of my cousin’s group had had an interaction with him. He was like, “Send us an EP.” This was the holy grail—this thing that you’re always reaching for. That was huge.

People really liked the melodic aspect of Bone Thugs, the speed of it. Ice Cube, Mack 10. The West Coast response to the East Coast. I would buy stuff from the East Coast because the lyricism—that type of rap where … We were trying to describe this in the story.

“Wordplay, poison darts.”

People like Chino XL, Crooked I, Black Thought, Kool G Rap. All these rapper’s rappers.Life After Deathhad a removableEXPLICITsticker. I remember I bought it, took it off, and I was in heaven, listening in my headphones in my room. Any of those lyricists. Canibus, Kurupt, Killah Priest, and Ras Kass—they didn’t have hit songs. The beats were very spare and they were just cutting loose over them.

So that’s what you were listening to. Was that different from what your cousin and those other guys were listening to?

I remember being in the studio for the first time. In high school I worked at the lake with my cousin, cleaning bathrooms. One day he’s like, “Just come by the studio.” They had this throwaway beat. “We’re not going to put a hook on it. You can just rap on it.” It wasn’t a good verse. I still remember it, but it wasn’t good. I was intimidated.

“By the way, you’re Silky Chad. Let’s see what you’ve got.” They used to tell you the name of the song, just like in the story.

And you just had to interpret it on the spot.

This is what Bone Thugs did. It’s what Cypress Hill did. It gives people creative freedom or whatever. The song was called “No Peace.”

I remember the verse I wrote was like, “There’s never any serenity / showing love and befriending me / but they’re never defending me / when there’s many an enemy / like Serbians to advance their plan / and put a bullet right through Franz Ferdinand / or when the people of France heard a man”—you know.

Super embarrassing. They let it go, but they’re also kind of looking at me askance, like, What are you talking about? We are rapping about no peace in these streets. Now when I listen to it, I’m cringing. I should’ve just rapped about punching someone’s brains in or something.

What happened after you got that invite from your cousin to the studio?

We were cleaning restrooms at Lake Piru, driving around in a golf cart. The fucking bathrooms were disgusting. Speaking of small towns, my mom’s first cousin got me the job at the lake. He was a dam keeper there. He also had a band, the Piru River Band. The music goes back generations. My grandparents’ generation were in the choir at the Catholic Church. My grandma played guitar.

Anyway, my cousin’s friends at the studio, they put out a CD before I ever went there. It was calledGet More to Fillmore. I remember thinking, This is dope. I was always wondering if my cousin would ask me to come, like, Why hasn’t he asked me? He’s older than me. And then he finally invited me.

The second CD was supposed to be calledFrom Struggle Comes Hustle. That one was supposed to go to Cowboy. So much care and effort went into it. A lot of tracks got made. Some of them are on the internet, like the one you heard. It never got finished. They started to lose people. They kept making songs, but if you don’t get a break, at some point, you’re just like, I’m forty. What do you do? I think they did it for a long time for the love of it.

It can’t be easy to produce a whole collection of actual songs like that, especially if there’s no money involved.

What happens to that stuff? It’s just in the wind. Stuff that gets made and doesn’t catch on. Even writing. There are so many things that you spend forever on and they still just sink to the bottom of the sea. I thought of music as my way into the culture.

But for people like my cousin, it was going to be the thing that got them out. If you stay in that small town for too long there’s only a few ways it can go. Some of them are bad. One reason why I’m always writing about these Chicano rap groups—we were always competing with one another. “We don’t wantthemto make it.” But then you look back and no one made it. No one made it out.

What do you think rap music means to Brad? Your identity as a rapper mirrors his in a way. There’s that very lonely scene where he’s rapping to himself and he’s flipping through all these CDs. What does he think about it?

One thing I was thinking about was, Is he good? I think it’s an interesting question. It’s not so good that people are like, Let’s sign Brad, but it’s not so bad that it’s like Dr. Seuss–type shit. On the one hand, it’s evident from the lyrics that the mechanics of rap are something that he’s thought about a lot. This is his artistic outlet, without him wanting to be conscious of it in that way.

It’s similar to me growing up. None of these guys that were making rap would’ve been like, I’m an artist. But that summer when my cousin finally invited me to the studio, and I did the Franz Ferdinand verse, I remember Mikey saying, “We gotta get in as many hooks as we can.” I was about to move away to college. But I would go—if I remember correctly—almost every day.

What was it like in the studio itself when you were working at that pace?

The studio was at my friend’s house, like in the story. It was a little converted closet. They’d glued empty egg cartons to the walls for insulation. One dude was just a wizard on the audio board. You’d pop on your headphones and he’d speak into your ear. I didn’t know anything about this, but when you layer tracks, you say something once and you say it over again so it thickens the voice. And you try to do it exactly the same every time.

I layered all these hooks they had me sing that way. Once, though, I thought it would be cool if the voice I did in the background was deeper. I remember, during layering for one song, I tried singing in this deep voice. They cut the track and the dude was like, “Ay. Nah.”

I was like, “Nah?”

Okay, got it—normal voice.
